user_input: Where should a user already registered for Microsoft Entra self-service password reset go to reset a forgotten password, and what if IT has not enabled self-service reset?
reference: Go to https://aka.ms/sspr. If IT has not enabled self-service password reset, contact the help desk for assistance.
reference_contexts: > This conceptual article explains to an administrator how self-service password reset works. If you're an end user already registered for self-service password reset and need to get back into your account, go to [https://aka.ms/sspr](https://aka.ms/sspr). > > If your IT team hasn't enabled the ability to reset your own password, reach out to your helpdesk for additional assistance.

user_input: An Entra SSPR policy changes from one required verification method to two. A user has only one method registered. Can that user still reset or unlock the account?
reference: No. With two verification methods required and only one registered, the user cannot reset or unlock the account. At least two properly configured methods are needed under that policy.
reference_contexts: If you start with a policy that has only one required authentication method for reset or unlock registered and you change that to two methods, what happens? | Number of methods registered | Number of methods required | Result | | :---: | :---: | :---: | | 1 or more | 1 | **Able** to reset or unlock | | 1 | 2 | **Unable** to reset or unlock | | 2 or more | 2 | **Able** to reset or unlock |

user_input: For accounts created and managed directly in Microsoft Entra ID, what password length and character-type requirements are listed in the password policy?
reference: Passwords must contain 8 to 256 characters and use at least three of four character types: lowercase letters, uppercase letters, numbers, and symbols.
reference_contexts:
| Password restrictions |A minimum of 8 characters and a maximum of 256 characters.
Requires three out of four of the following types of characters:
- Lowercase characters
- Uppercase characters
- Numbers (0-9)
- Symbols (see the previous password restrictions) |

user_input: Under the administrator two-gate SSPR policy, how many pieces of authentication data are required, and can security questions be used?
reference: Two pieces of authentication data are required, such as an email address, an authenticator app, or a phone number. Security questions are prohibited.
reference_contexts: The two-gate policy requires two pieces of authentication data, such as an email address, authenticator app, or a phone number, and it prohibits security questions. Office and mobile voice calls are also prohibited for trial or free versions of Microsoft Entra ID.

user_input: According to the Entra SSPR troubleshooting guide, what should be checked when an administrator cannot see Password reset under Protection?
reference: Check whether a Microsoft Entra ID license is assigned to the administrator performing the operation. The guide identifies a missing license on that administrator as the reason the Password reset option is not visible.
reference_contexts: You don't see **Password reset** if you don't have a Microsoft Entra ID license assigned to the administrator performing the operation.

user_input: My Entra password-reset phone call never arrives, and my directory phone number includes an extension. What does the troubleshooting guide say to fix?
reference: Check that the directory phone number is correctly formatted, for example +1 4251234567. Password reset does not support extensions and strips them before calling. Use a number without an extension or integrate the extension into the phone number in the PBX.
reference_contexts:
| The user never receives the password reset SMS or phone call. | The phone number in the directory may be malformed. Make sure the phone number is in the format "+1 4251234567".

Password reset doesn't support extensions, even if you specify one in the directory. The extensions are stripped before the call is made. Use a number without an extension, or integrate the extension into the phone number in your private branch exchange (PBX). |

user_input: For Microsoft Entra Connect version 1.1.443.0 or later in the global Azure cloud, which outbound HTTPS destinations are required for password writeback?
reference: Outbound HTTPS access is required to *.passwordreset.microsoftonline.com and *.servicebus.windows.net.
reference_contexts: For Microsoft Entra Connect version *1.1.443.0* and higher, *outbound HTTPS* access is required to the following addresses: * *\*.passwordreset.microsoftonline.com* * *\*.servicebus.windows.net*

user_input: Which event IDs help identify the service bus listener for Entra password-writeback troubleshooting, and how can its port connectivity be tested?
reference: On the Entra Connect server, inspect the Windows Application event log for event ID 31034 or 31019 and identify the service bus listener namespace. Test it with Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <namespace>.servicebus.windows.net -Port 443.
reference_contexts: 1. On the Entra connect server, open the event viewer logs (Windows logs, application) and locate one of these event IDs: 31034 or 31019. 1. From these Event IDs, identify the name of the service bus listener:
Test-NetConnection -ComputerName <namespace>.servicebus.windows.net -Port 443

user_input: Can an Azure subscription with pay-as-you-go pricing enable a spending limit?
reference: No. Spending limits are unavailable for pay-as-you-go subscriptions and subscriptions with commitment plans. The portal does not show a spending limit for these subscriptions, and one cannot be enabled.
reference_contexts: The spending limit isn’t available for subscriptions with commitment plans or with pay-as-you-go pricing. For those types of subscriptions, a spending limit isn't shown in the Azure portal and you can't enable one. See the full list of Azure subscription types and the availability of the spending limit.

user_input: If I leave the Azure spending limit enabled, does that guarantee that every type of charge is blocked?
reference: No. Some external services published in Azure Marketplace cannot use subscription credits and can incur separate charges even when a spending limit is set. Examples listed include Visual Studio licenses, Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2, support plans, and most third-party branded services.
reference_contexts: Some external services published in the Azure Marketplace can't be used with your subscription credits, and can incur separate charges even when your spending limit is set. Examples include Visual Studio licenses, Microsoft Entra ID P1 or P2, support plans, and most third-party branded services. When you create a new external service, a warning is shown to let you know the services are billed separately:

user_input: For an Azure MOSP subscription invoice, who can download it, and are subscription Owner, Contributor, or Reader roles sufficient by themselves?
reference: The subscription account administrator can download the invoice. Users with subscription Owner, Contributor, or Reader roles can download it only if the account administrator grants permission; those roles alone are not sufficient.
reference_contexts: You must have an account admin role for a subscription to download its invoice. Users with owner, contributor, or reader roles can download its invoice, if the account admin gives them permission. For more information, see Allow users to download invoices.

user_input: Which roles allow downloading an Azure MCA or MPA billing-profile invoice, and who can download invoices for all billing profiles in an account?
reference: An Owner, Contributor, Reader, or Invoice Manager on the billing profile can download that profile's invoice. An Owner, Contributor, or Reader on the billing account can download invoices for every billing profile in that account.
reference_contexts: You must have an owner, contributor, reader, or an invoice manager role on a billing profile to download its invoice in the Azure portal. Users with an owner, contributor, or a reader role on a billing account can download invoices for all the billing profiles in the account.

user_input: After paying a past-due Azure balance, how long can subscription reactivation take, and when should a continuing resource-management delay be escalated?
reference: Reactivation can take up to 24 hours after payment. Once the subscription is reactivated, if a delay in creating or managing resources exceeds 30 minutes, contact Azure Billing Support. Most resources resume automatically, but check them and restart them if needed.
reference_contexts: It can take up to 24 hours for your subscription to get reactivated after you pay your balance. After reactivation After your subscription is reactivated, there might be a delay in creating or managing resources. If the delay exceeds 30 minutes, contact Azure Billing Support for assistance. Most Azure resources automatically resume and don't require any action. However, we recommend that you check your Azure service resources and restart them if, if necessary.

user_input: Does requesting an Azure quota increase itself cost money, and does an assigned adjustable quota guarantee resource capacity?
reference: There is no charge for requesting a quota increase; charges depend on resource usage. An adjustable-quota increase is subject to Microsoft's review, including usage, service availability, and capacity constraints. An assigned quota does not reserve or guarantee capacity.
reference_contexts: There's no cost associated with requesting a quota increase. Costs are based on resource usage, not the quotas themselves.

Adjustable quotas: Quotas for which you can request quota increases fall into this category. Each subscription has a default quota value for each quota. Microsoft may review and adjust Quotas from time to time, including increasing or decreasing Quotas based on Customer usage patterns or where allocated Quotas are not utilized. You can request an increase for an adjustable quota from the Azure Home My quotas page, providing an amount or usage percentage and submitting it directly. This is the quickest way to increase quotas. Approval of such requests is subject to Microsoft's review, including consideration of current usage, service availability, and capacity constraints. An assigned Quota does not reserve or guarantee capacity for Customer use, and capacity may not be available at the time of request.

user_input: Under RFC 6749 section 4.1.2, how long should an authorization code live, and what must happen if it is used more than once?
reference: The code must expire shortly after issuance; a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes is recommended. The client must not use it more than once. If it is reused, the authorization server must deny the request and should revoke, when possible, all tokens previously issued from that code.
reference_contexts: code REQUIRED. The authorization code generated by the authorization server. The authorization code MUST expire shortly after it is issued to mitigate the risk of leaks. A maximum authorization code lifetime of 10 minutes is RECOMMENDED. The client MUST NOT use the authorization code Hardt Standards Track [Page 26] RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 October 2012 more than once. If an authorization code is used more than once, the authorization server MUST deny the request and SHOULD revoke (when possible) all tokens previously issued based on that authorization code. The authorization code is bound to the client identifier and redirection URI.

user_input: In an RFC 7009 token revocation request, which body parameter is required, which token-type hint is optional, and what happens if the hint does not locate the token?
reference: The token parameter is required, while token_type_hint is optional. The request body uses application/x-www-form-urlencoded. If the server cannot find the token using the hint, it must search across all token types it supports; it may also ignore the hint.
reference_contexts: The client constructs the request by including the following parameters using the "application/x-www-form-urlencoded" format in the HTTP request entity-body: token REQUIRED. The token that the client wants to get revoked. token_type_hint OPTIONAL. A hint about the type of the token submitted for revocation. Clients MAY pass this parameter in order to help the authorization server to optimize the token lookup. If the server is unable to locate the token using the given hint, it MUST extend its search across all of its supported token types. An authorization server MAY ignore this parameter, particularly if it is able to detect the token type automatically. This specification defines two such values: * access_token: An access token as defined in [RFC6749], Section 1.4 * refresh_token: A refresh token as defined in [RFC6749], Section 1.5

user_input: A client sends an invalid token to an RFC 7009 revocation endpoint. Should the endpoint return an invalid-token error?
reference: No. The server returns HTTP 200 both when revocation succeeds and when the submitted token is invalid. Invalid tokens do not cause an error response, and the client ignores the response body. An invalid token_type_hint value is also ignored.
reference_contexts: The authorization server responds with HTTP status code 200 if the token has been revoked successfully or if the client submitted an invalid token. Lodderstedt, et al. Standards Track [Page 5] RFC 7009 Token Revocation August 2013 Note: invalid tokens do not cause an error response since the client cannot handle such an error in a reasonable way. Moreover, the purpose of the revocation request, invalidating the particular token, is already achieved. The content of the response body is ignored by the client as all necessary information is conveyed in the response code. An invalid token type hint value is ignored by the authorization server and does not influence the revocation response.

user_input: Under RFC 7662, what should an authorized introspection response contain when the token is inactive, unknown, or not available for that protected resource to introspect?
reference: The authorization server must return active set to false. To avoid disclosing its state, it should not provide additional information about the inactive token, including the reason it is inactive.
reference_contexts: If the introspection call is properly authorized but the token is not active, does not exist on this server, or the protected resource is not allowed to introspect this particular token, then the authorization server MUST return an introspection response with the "active" field set to "false". Note that to avoid disclosing too much of the authorization server's state to a third party, the authorization server SHOULD NOT include any additional information about an inactive token, including why the token is inactive.

user_input: For the RFC 8628 device authorization flow, how should a client poll after authorization_pending, and how does slow_down change the interval?
reference: After authorization_pending, the client should keep polling but must wait at least the interval supplied in the device authorization response, or 5 seconds if none was supplied. After slow_down, polling can continue, but the interval must increase by 5 seconds for that request and all subsequent requests.
reference_contexts: authorization_pending The authorization request is still pending as the end user hasn't yet completed the user-interaction steps (Section 3.3). The client SHOULD repeat the access token request to the token endpoint (a process known as polling). Before each new request, the client MUST wait at least the number of seconds specified by the "interval" parameter of the device authorization response (see Section 3.2), or 5 seconds if none was provided, and respect any increase in the polling interval required by the "slow_down" error. slow_down A variant of "authorization_pending", the authorization request is still pending and polling should continue, but the interval MUST be increased by 5 seconds for this and all subsequent requests.

user_input: According to RFC 9068, must JWT access tokens be signed, may they use alg=none, and which signature algorithm must conforming servers support?
reference: JWT access tokens must be signed and must not use none as the signing algorithm. Conforming authorization servers and resource servers must support RS256. Asymmetric cryptography is recommended, rather than being the only signing approach the profile permits.
reference_contexts: JWT access tokens MUST be signed. Although JWT access tokens can use any signing algorithm, use of asymmetric cryptography is RECOMMENDED as it simplifies the process of acquiring validation information for resource servers (see Section 4). JWT access tokens MUST NOT use "none" as the signing algorithm. See Section 4 for more details. Authorization servers and resource servers conforming to this specification MUST include RS256 (as defined in [RFC7518]) among their supported signature algorithms.

user_input: What typ header value does RFC 9068 recommend for JWT access tokens, and why explicitly distinguish them from ID tokens?
reference: The recommended typ value is at+jwt, omitting the application/ prefix from application/at+jwt. Explicit access-token typing helps prevent a resource server from accepting an OpenID Connect ID token as an access token.
reference_contexts: This specification registers the "application/at+jwt" media type, which can be used to indicate that the content is a JWT access token. JWT access tokens MUST include this media type in the "typ" header parameter to explicitly declare that the JWT represents an access token complying with this profile. Per the definition of "typ" in Section 4.1.9 of [RFC7515], it is RECOMMENDED that the "application/" prefix be omitted. Therefore, the "typ" value used SHOULD be "at+jwt". See the Security Considerations section for details on the importance of preventing OpenID Connect ID Tokens (as defined by Section 2 of [OpenID.Core]) from being accepted as access tokens by resource servers implementing this profile.

user_input: What does a successful RFC 9126 pushed authorization request return, and what restrictions apply to the request_uri?
reference: The server returns HTTP 201 with a JSON response containing request_uri and expires_in. request_uri is a single-use reference to the posted authorization request and must be bound to the client that posted it. expires_in is its lifetime in seconds as a positive integer; the server chooses the lifetime, which is typically short, for example 5 to 600 seconds.
reference_contexts: If the verification is successful, the server MUST generate a request URI and provide it in the response with a 201 HTTP status code. The following parameters are included as top-level members in the message body of the HTTP response using the application/json media type as defined by [RFC8259]. request_uri The request URI corresponding to the authorization request posted. This URI is a single-use reference to the respective request data in the subsequent authorization request. The way the authorization process obtains the authorization request data is at the discretion of the authorization server and is out of scope of this specification. There is no need to make the authorization request data available to other parties via this URI. expires_in A JSON number that represents the lifetime of the request URI in seconds as a positive integer. The request URI lifetime is at the discretion of the authorization server but will typically be relatively short (e.g., between 5 and 600 seconds).
The request_uri value MUST be bound to the client that posted the authorization request.

user_input: Which JOSE header fields must an RFC 9449 DPoP proof JWT contain, and what algorithm and key-content restrictions apply?
reference: It must contain typ with value dpop+jwt, alg identifying an asymmetric JWS signature algorithm, and jwk containing the client's public key. alg must not be none or a symmetric MAC algorithm, and jwk must not contain a private key.
reference_contexts: A DPoP proof is a JWT [RFC7519] that is signed (using JSON Web Signature (JWS) [RFC7515]) with a private key chosen by the client (see below). The JOSE Header of a DPoP JWT MUST contain at least the following parameters: typ: A field with the value dpop+jwt, which explicitly types the DPoP proof JWT as recommended in Section 3.11 of [RFC8725]. alg: An identifier for a JWS asymmetric digital signature algorithm from [IANA.JOSE.ALGS]. It MUST NOT be none or an identifier for a symmetric algorithm (Message Authentication Code (MAC)). jwk: Represents the public key chosen by the client in JSON Web Key (JWK) [RFC7517] format as defined in Section 4.1.3 of [RFC7515]. It MUST NOT contain a private key.

user_input: In RFC 9449, what do htm, htu, and iat identify in a DPoP proof, and how is ath calculated when an access token is presented to a protected resource?
reference: htm identifies the HTTP method, htu identifies the target URI without query or fragment, and iat is the proof's creation timestamp. When the proof accompanies an access token for protected-resource access, ath is also required: it is the base64url-encoded SHA-256 hash of the ASCII encoding of the access token's value.
reference_contexts: htm: The value of the HTTP method (Section 9.1 of [RFC9110]) of the request to which the JWT is attached. htu: The HTTP target URI (Section 7.1 of [RFC9110]) of the request to which the JWT is attached, without query and fragment parts. iat: Creation timestamp of the JWT (Section 4.1.6 of [RFC7519]). When the DPoP proof is used in conjunction with the presentation of an access token in protected resource access (see Section 7), the DPoP proof MUST also contain the following claim: ath: Hash of the access token. The value MUST be the result of a base64url encoding (as defined in Section 2 of [RFC7515]) the SHA-256 [SHS] hash of the ASCII encoding of the associated access token's value.

user_input: How did guidance on the OAuth resource owner password credentials grant change from RFC 6749 section 4.3 to RFC 9700 section 2.4?
reference: RFC 6749 described the password credentials grant for cases where the resource owner trusts the client and other flows are not viable. RFC 9700 updates the guidance and says the grant must not be used because it exposes user credentials to clients, expands the attack surface, and is not designed for two-factor authentication or multi-step authentication. This is newer security guidance superseding the older allowance, not two equally current policies to choose between.
reference_contexts: The resource owner password credentials grant type is suitable in cases where the resource owner has a trust relationship with the client, such as the device operating system or a highly privileged Hardt Standards Track [Page 37] RFC 6749 OAuth 2.0 October 2012 application. The authorization server should take special care when enabling this grant type and only allow it when other flows are not viable.

The resource owner password credentials grant [RFC6749] MUST NOT be used. This grant type insecurely exposes the credentials of the resource owner to the client. Even if the client is benign, usage of this grant results in an increased attack surface (i.e., credentials can leak in more places than just the authorization server) and in training users to enter their credentials in places other than the authorization server. Furthermore, the resource owner password credentials grant is not designed to work with two- factor authentication and authentication processes that require multiple user interaction steps. Authentication with cryptographic credentials (cf. WebCrypto [W3C.WebCrypto], WebAuthn [W3C.WebAuthn]) may be impossible to implement with this grant type, as it is usually bound to a specific web origin.
